Senses.Explanation: Literally, to receive or meet (接) and lead (引): "to receive and lead." The compound occurs 501 times in 170 allowlisted texts. In Chan records it commonly names a master's reception of students and the answers given when they come before him. Asked, "how do you receive and lead?" (作麼生接引), one master answers, "every house has a road open to carts and horses" (家家有路通車馬). Another, asked "by which gate do you receive and lead later students?" (以那一門接引後學), answers with the recorded alternatives of staff and shout, expedient and actual, opposing and following. A monk who says, "I too hope to be received and led" (某甲亦望接引), is told, "one cannot walk by taking another by the hand; only one's own assent is intimate" (把手牽人行不得，為人自肯乃方親). Another record asks whether the fundamental matter can be used to receive people, then sets "if there is receiving" against "without relying on receiving" (若有接引；不假接引). Thus the corpus uses an ordinary verb of reception as a category for a master's dealings with arrivals, while also recording challenges to the category itself; it supplies no single fixed procedure under the word.
Senses.Note: Late allowlisted records also use the same verb for buddhas receiving beings or the dead into a pure land. Those are not used to define this Chan entry. The reception pavilion (接引閣) is a building name and is likewise excluded from the lexical evidence.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：「學人不服諸方胡棒亂喝，喜今日親覲，和尚作麼生接引？」師云：「家家有路通車馬。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public interview asks how the master receives and leads; he answers, "every house has a road open to carts and horses."

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：「十方婆伽梵，一路涅槃門，和尚以那一門接引後學？」師云：「棒喝兩途，權實雙舉，逆之順之，凡聖皆取。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The question asks by which gate the master receives later students; the answer enumerates staff and shout, expedient and actual, opposing and following.

Occurrences.Kwic: 還堪以本分事接引否？若有接引，不名本分；不假接引，本分誰名？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The passage explicitly tests receiving against the fundamental matter: if there is receiving it is not called fundamental; without receiving, who names the fundamental?

Occurrences.Kwic: 只要諸人各自直下承當，隨方接引不負來機，者便是病僧一片真實心腸
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The speaker joins each person's own direct acceptance to receiving according to circumstances without failing the arriving capacity.

Senses.Explanation: Gruel (粥) is the thin cooked-grain meal served in the monastery, ordinarily the morning member of the recurring pair ‘gruel and rice’ (粥飯). The word retains that concrete referent throughout the record: the monastic code directs that opening the bowl and eating gruel or rice, tea or broth, must be done carefully and in order (展鉢喫粥喫飰或茶或湯，皆須細齊整), and a kitchen exchange distinguishes cooking gruel from steaming rice (煮粥耶？蒸飯耶？). Chan bends this everyday meal by repeatedly putting it into public answers and named cases. Asked for ‘talk that surpasses buddhas and patriarchs,’ Changping answers ‘eating gruel and eating rice’ (喫粥喫飯); asked about the student's own self, Guizong answers ‘when the gruel is thin, sit down later’ (粥稀後坐). In Zhaozhou's case, a newly arrived monk asks for instruction; Zhaozhou asks, ‘have you eaten your gruel?’ (喫粥了也未), and after the monk says he has, tells him, ‘go wash your bowl’ (洗鉢盂去). Yunmen preserves the exchange and explicitly asks whether Zhaozhou gave an instruction. Later records repeatedly quote and comment on the same question-and-answer. The meal also supplies the record's language for the ordinary allotment: Baichi says ‘eating gruel and eating rice is your own basic lot’ (喫粥喫飯是汝本分事), while a Zhaozhou saying names the two daily gruel-and-rice meals as his only occasion of ‘mixed use of mind’ (除二時粥飯是雜用心處). In the Ganzhi–Nanquan case, Ganzhi provides gruel and requests the meal recitation; Nanquan dedicates it to ‘the tabby cat and white ox’ (貍奴白牯), after which Ganzhi leaves and Nanquan breaks the cooking pot. Thus the corpus does not turn gruel into a second object or an abstract substance: it keeps the food concrete while deploying eating, serving, and washing up in answers, institutional schedules, and public cases.
Senses.Note: Zen-allowlist concordance: gruel (粥) has 2,824 hits in 341 files; eat gruel (喫粥) 748/182; gruel and rice (粥飯) 668/223; ‘have you eaten your gruel?’ (喫粥了也未) 101/67; and gruel-and-rice monk (粥飯僧) 59/42. No definition-formula search supplied a definition of the food: ‘what is gruel?’ (如何是粥), ‘so-called gruel’ (所謂粥), ‘termed gruel’ (謂之粥), ‘named gruel’ (名為粥), and ‘called gruel’ (喚作粥) all returned zero. The 18 hits for the grammatical string ‘as for gruel’ or ‘one who handles gruel’ (粥者) occur in contexts such as ‘the one serving gruel’ or inside the named phrase ‘Jiang's thin gruel’; they are not definitions. Sense audit: ordinary breakfast gruel, offered or cooked gruel, and the gruel in Zhaozhou's case are the same food, hence one sense. Related entries should keep separate the eating bowl (鉢盂) from the robe-and-bowl succession token (衣鉢), and should give the scorn epithet ‘gruel-and-rice monk’ (粥飯僧) its own lexical article rather than assigning that human referent to the standalone word ‘gruel’ (粥).

Occurrences.Kwic: 堂中座位衣單掛鉢展鉢喫粥喫飰或茶或湯。皆須󱶂細齊整。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Monastic Regulations for the Chan Garden, in its section on the head seat, treats eating gruel as an ordered communal meal: opening the bowl and eating gruel, rice, tea, or broth must be done carefully and neatly. This anchors the institutional deployment and the concrete food sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉僧問趙州。某甲乍入叢林。乞師指示。州云。喫粥了也未。僧云。喫粥了也。州云。洗鉢盂去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yunmen's record quotes the complete Zhaozhou exchange: the newcomer asks for instruction, Zhaozhou asks whether he has eaten his gruel, and then tells him to go wash his bowl. The following lines have Yunmen ask whether an instruction was given.

Occurrences.Kwic: 喫粥喫飯是汝本分事
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Baichi's record places eating gruel and rice in a series of ordinary activities and calls it ‘your own basic lot.’ The local speaker was not independently resolved, so the master field remains unset.

Occurrences.Kwic: 今早起來。無言可說。下牀著鞋。後架洗面。堂內展鉢喫粥。粥後打睡。睡起喫茶。見客相喚。齋時喫飯。日日相似。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Fayan's lamp-record section lists the ordinary daily sequence: rise, put on shoes, wash, open the bowl and eat gruel in the hall, sleep after gruel, drink tea, greet guests, and eat rice at mealtime—‘each day alike.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰汝炊飯耶煮粥耶。對曰。人工淘米著火。行者煮粥炊飯。曰汝作甚麼。對曰。和尚慈悲放他閑去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the kitchen exchange in the Continued Transmission of the Lamp, Touzi asks Daokai whether he steams rice or cooks gruel. Daokai assigns washing rice and lighting the fire to workmen, and cooking gruel and rice to attendants. It independently anchors preparation of the literal meal.

Occurrences.Kwic: 老僧行脚時，除二時粥飯是雜用心處，除外更無別用心處。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The collected outlines quote Zhaozhou: while travelling, apart from the two daily gruel-and-rice meals as occasions of mixed use of mind, he had no other such occasion. This anchors the institutional two-meal formula.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問。如何是超佛越祖之談。師曰。喫粥喫飯。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Changping's lamp-record section, a monk asks what talk surpasses buddhas and patriarchs; the answer is ‘eating gruel and eating rice.’ This anchors gruel as the content of a public answer without assigning an unstated interpretation to it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。如何是學人自己。師曰。牀窄先臥。粥稀後坐。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Asked about the student's own self, Guizong Daoquan answers with the paired household maxim: ‘when the bed is narrow, lie down first; when the gruel is thin, sit down later.’ This anchors ordinary gruel inside an attested public answer.

Occurrences.Kwic: 又於南泉設粥云請和尚念誦南泉云甘贄行者設粥請大眾為貍奴白牯念摩訶般若波羅蜜甘乃禮拜便出去南泉却到厨內打破鍋子
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The abridged transmission record preserves the Ganzhi–Nanquan case: Ganzhi provides gruel and asks Nanquan to recite; Nanquan announces a dedication for the tabby cat and white ox; Ganzhi leaves, and Nanquan breaks the pot in the kitchen.

Senses.Explanation: The joined food words are also the institutional name for a monastery's scheduled meals and food support. The monastic code schedules “gruel and rice at the two meal-times; tea and hot water at the third” (二時上粥飯。三時上茶湯). Zhaozhou likewise identifies “the two gruel-and-rice meals” (二時粥飯) as the only occasions that divided his attention while travelling. An abbot calls himself a “gruel-and-rice host” (粥飯主人), receiving travellers with salt, vinegar, enough gruel, and enough rice. In these passages the headword does not merely inventory two foods: it names the recurring communal provision, its times, and the host responsible for it.
Senses.Note: The allowlisted concordance has 668 hits in 223 texts. Institutional families include the two gruel-and-rice meal-times (二時粥飯), gruel-and-rice circumstances or support (粥飯因緣), and the gruel-and-rice host (粥飯主人). These are deployments of one communal meal system, not separate senses. The institution is distinct from the physical gruel and cooked rice in the literal sense below.

Occurrences.Kwic: 二時上粥飯。三時上茶湯。大眾諷經
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Imperially Revised Baizhang Monastic Code gives an institutional schedule: gruel and rice at two times, tea and hot water at three.

Occurrences.Kwic: 老僧行脚時。除二時粥飯是雜用心處。除外更無別用心處。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhaozhou says that during his travels only the two scheduled gruel-and-rice meals were mixed employment of mind.

Occurrences.Kwic: 推向十字路頭住箇破院，作粥飯主人接待南北，事不獲已，隨分有鹽有醋、粥足飯足。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An abbot describes being made to inhabit a ruined monastery as the gruel-and-rice host who receives travellers from north and south and maintains the meal provision.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, the first graph names gruel and the second cooked rice or a rice meal. The corpus uses the pair as physical food: a verse says that mountain-field gruel and rice smell fragrant, and a discourse observes that after three days without being fed gruel and rice a person cannot move, but can move after eating some. Another address enumerates eating gruel and eating rice beside relieving oneself, walking, sitting, and sleeping as the listener's own fundamental matter. The rebuke “puffing gruel-and-rice breath” (鼓粥飯氣) is a food-derived fixed compound; it depends on consumed food but does not turn the literal food pair into the institutional schedule above.
Senses.Note: Literal food predicates include eating, being fed, smelling fragrant, and having enough gruel and rice. The gruel-and-rice breath phrase (粥飯氣) and the gruel-and-rice monk (粥飯僧) are longer compounds and remain separate lexical articles or families. Their existence does not collapse physical food into the communal meal system.

Occurrences.Kwic: 參禪學道是汝本分事、喫粥喫飯是汝本分事、屙屎撒尿是汝本分事、行坐打眠是汝本分事
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The speaker enumerates eating gruel and cooked rice among ordinary bodily activities called the listener's own fundamental matter.

Occurrences.Kwic: 設問答到彌勒下生，勾鎖連環，盛水不漏，也祇是空鼓粥飯氣，於自己了沒交涉。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The rebuke calls flawless linked question-and-answer merely empty puffing of gruel-and-rice breath, preserving a fixed compound derived from consumed food.

Occurrences.Kwic: 繭紙衣裳軟，山田粥飯香，此生隨分過，無可得思量。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The verse says, ‘Silkworm-paper clothes are soft; mountain-field gruel and rice are fragrant.’ Fragrance is a predicate of the physical food.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不與粥飯喫三日時還動得麼定是動不得也纔方喫得些粥飯方能動得
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The discourse asks whether someone unfed gruel and rice for three days can still move, then says that after eating some gruel and rice the person can move. The predicate is bodily nourishment by physical food.

Senses.Explanation: In institutional self-description, “gruel-and-rice monk” names an ordinary resident who remains within the monastery's communal support rather than accepting a public or abbatial post. One master, repeatedly summoned by governors to prestigious monasteries, says, “I am a long-term gruel-and-rice monk; transmitting the buddha-mind lineage is no small matter” (我長行粥飯僧，傳佛心宗非細事也) and refuses eight invitations. Another declines an invitation to lead Nanyuan by saying, “I have long been a gruel-and-rice monk and vow not to emerge into the human world” (我長作粥飯僧，誓不願出人間世矣). A third master answers a question about himself simply, “If you ask me, I am a gruel-and-rice monk” (若問我，我則粥飯僧). These passages use the compound as an institutional identity, not as a literal claim that the monk does nothing except eat.
Senses.Note: The headword has 59 hits in 42 allowlisted texts. Refusal of abbacy or public emergence and plain self-identification establish the ordinary-resident sense. Long-term or regular forms (長行粥飯僧 and 常行粥飯僧) must be assigned by context: they can name this resident identity or the eating-only classification below.

Occurrences.Kwic: 未委和尚如何？」師云：「若問我，我則粥飯僧。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Asked how it is with him, the master replies, ‘If you ask me, I am a gruel-and-rice monk.’ The self-description names his ordinary resident identity.

Occurrences.Kwic: 乃曰我長行粥飯僧傳佛心宗非細事也前後八請堅臥不荅
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After governors press him to accept prestigious monasteries, the master calls himself a long-term gruel-and-rice monk and refuses eight invitations.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰：我長作粥飯僧，誓不願出人間世矣。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Invited to lead Nanyuan, the master says, ‘I have long been a gruel-and-rice monk and vow not to emerge into the human world.’

Senses.PreferredTarget: a monk who merely eats communal meals
Senses.Explanation: In a separate literal and contrastive classification, the compound denotes a monk characterized as consuming the community's gruel and rice without the activity set against it. An official asks whether Weishan's assembly consists of “monks who eat gruel and rice” or “monks who investigate Chan” (喫粥飯僧 / 參禪僧); Weishan rejects both offered categories. Zhenjing tells the assembly not to become “long-term gruel-and-rice monks” (不可作長行粥飯僧). Xiangyan says that he will cease studying the buddha teaching and become such a monk, sparing his mind the labor. Later records reuse the same eat-versus-study contrast. Here the headword classifies a monk by meal consumption, not by the non-abbatial institutional identity in the primary sense.
Senses.Note: Dismissive external use, self-directed use, and Weishan's refusal are readings within this meal-consuming classification, not further senses. The gruel-and-rice food pair (粥飯), rice-bag fellow (飯袋子), and wine-lees fellow (酒糟漢) are related but lexically distinct. Eating gruel and rice in one's own fundamental matter (本分事) does not by itself apply this classification to a monk.

Occurrences.Kwic: 既到㱕宗門下須是一箇箇心空及第㱕不可作長行粥飯僧
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The assembly is told not to become long-term gruel-and-rice monks; the prohibition supplies the dismissive classification.

Occurrences.Kwic: 為復是喫粥飯僧。為復是參禪僧。師云。亦不是喫粥飯僧。亦不是參禪僧。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An official contrasts monks who eat gruel and rice with monks who investigate Chan; Weishan answers that the assembly is neither.

Occurrences.Kwic: 此生不學佛法也。且作箇長行粥飯僧。免役心神。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xiangyan says he will cease studying the buddha teaching and become a long-term gruel-and-rice monk, sparing his mind the labor.

Occurrences.Kwic: 長為粥飯僧，不復學識；做個癡獃漢，必要明心。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later couplet pairs remaining a gruel-and-rice monk with no longer pursuing learned knowledge, preserving the meal-consuming versus study contrast.

Senses.Explanation: The graphs name a mustard seed. The allowlisted corpus has 442 hits in 146 texts. Its small size supplies the comparison ‘mustard-seed-sized’ (芥子許, 67 hits in 50 texts), as when a teacher speaks of a doubt as small as a mustard seed. The corpus also repeatedly pairs the seed with Mount Sumeru in both directions: ‘Sumeru contains a mustard seed’ (須彌納芥子, 46 hits in 30 texts) and ‘a mustard seed contains Sumeru’ (芥子納須彌, 59 hits in 44 texts). In the Guizong encounter, Li Bo accepts the first statement but asks whether the second is false; Guizong asks where Li Bo’s ten thousand books are held in a body the size of a coconut. In another exchange, the two directions receive the one-word answers ‘easy’ and ‘difficult.’ A later address records mountains, earth, trees, monastics, laypeople, sages, and ordinary people placed inside a mustard seed without the seed becoming narrow. These are the corpus’s recorded scale constructions; the entry does not turn them into a symbolic meaning for the seed.
Senses.Note: All required definition formulas were searched. One ‘What is the mustard seed?’ question is included because its answer, ‘It blocks your eye,’ is an attested direct response, not adopted here as a universal lexical equation. Deployment inventory includes the small-measure construction, both Sumeru constructions, question-and-answer use, and a later expanded list of what is placed inside the seed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 教中所言。須彌納芥子。㴾即不疑。芥子納須彌。莫是妄譚否。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Li Bo contrasts the two directions of the Sumeru-and-mustard-seed statement in his question to Guizong.

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰。如何是芥子。師曰。塞將汝眼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Shishi Shandao’s section, the teacher answers ‘What is the mustard seed?’ with ‘It blocks your eye.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 若有一疑如芥子許，是汝真善知識。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Daomin’s address uses a mustard seed as the size comparison for a doubt.

Occurrences.Kwic: 將山河大地、艸木叢林、若僧若俗、若聖若凡納入芥子，而芥子不見其窄。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A winter-retreat conclusion places an enumerated world inside a mustard seed and says the seed does not become narrow.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：如何是芥子納須彌？王云：易。問：如何是須彌納芥子？王云：難。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A paired exchange asks about each direction and records the king’s answers ‘easy’ and ‘difficult.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 須彌芥子父。芥子須彌爺。山水坦然平。敲氷來煮茶。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu quotes Fu Dashi’s reciprocal father-and-grandfather wording for Sumeru and the mustard seed.
